justice: Road space is heavily allocated to motor vehicles (multiple wide lanes with turn arrows), while pedestrian realm is not clearly visible, suggesting an imbalanced distribution of space for non-drivers.
Clear lane markings and standardized traffic signs (yield sign and right-turn mandatory sign) indicate rule clarity that generally applies equally across users.

A curb and landscaped verge are present on the right, but the sidewalk/crossing access features (curb ramps, tactile paving) are not visible, limiting confidence in barrier-free accessibility for all users.
safety: Prominent zebra crosswalk markings ahead provide a defined pedestrian crossing zone and reduce ambiguity at the intersection approach.
Directional arrows and solid lane lines organize turning movements, reducing side-swipe and merge conflicts among drivers approaching the intersection.

The intersection appears wide with multiple turning paths and no visible pedestrian refuge island or signal heads in frame, which can increase exposure time for pedestrians and raise conflict risk with turning vehicles.
livability: The streetscape is dominated by vehicle infrastructure (wide asphalt area and turning lanes), with limited visible street-level destinations or active frontages, reducing day-to-day vibrancy.
Greenery is present (trees, shrubs, and grass on the right and in the median area), which supports a more pleasant environment for staying and passing through.
No visible benches, plazas, or gathering features near the crossing area, limiting opportunities for lingering or social interaction for all users.
sustainability: Substantial roadside and median vegetation (trees and shrubs) contributes to carbon sequestration and urban habitat compared with a fully paved corridor.
No visible dedicated cycling facility (protected lane, bike symbols, or physical separation), which may discourage low-carbon mode shift to cycling.
The corridor design emphasizes smooth vehicle flow (wide lanes and large turning radii), which can induce higher vehicle use and speeds, weakening transport sustainability outcomes.
aesthetics: Mature trees and layered planting (tree canopy with trimmed shrubs) create a visually orderly green edge along the roadway.
The scene appears clean and well-maintained (clear markings, maintained landscaping, and uncluttered roadside), improving overall visual quality.
Large expanses of asphalt and the visual presence of elevated infrastructure in the background make the view feel more highway-like than street-like, reducing human-scale appeal.

Large open asphalt area and limited shading over the roadway and crossing zone likely increase heat exposure for anyone walking/cycling across or waiting to cross.
Landscaped buffer (grass/shrubs) between road and the right-side edge can improve perceived comfort by creating separation from traffic, though seating or shelters are not visible.

bikeability: No visible bike lane markings, colored pavement, or protective separation, indicating low cycling prioritization and higher perceived risk for cyclists.
Wide multi-lane intersection approach with turning movements (multiple turn arrows) increases potential conflicts with cyclists, particularly with right-turning vehicles.
Road edge treatment is landscaped with a curb, but there is no clearly designated cycling space adjacent to it, limiting comfort and route legibility for everyday cycling.
